q: Solutions of MgCl<sub>2</sub> and NaOH were mixed, and Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>(s) formed by the reaction shown. The box shows everything present after the reaction stopped (water not shown). Each cluster of one Mg<sup>2+</sup> with two OH<sup>−</sup> is one unit of the solid. How many formula units of each reactant were mixed?
h: Atoms and ions are conserved. Count every Mg²⁺, Cl⁻, Na⁺ and OH⁻ in the box, both in the solid and dissolved.
w: The box holds 3 Mg(OH)2 units plus 1 dissolved Mg2+, 6 Na+ and 8 Cl−. Total Mg2+ = 4 and Cl− = 8, which is 4 MgCl2. Total OH− = 6 (all in the solid) and Na+ = 6, which is 6 NaOH. So 4 MgCl2 and 6 NaOH were mixed, and MgCl2 was in excess (1 Mg2+ is left over). Answers with 3 MgCl2 miss the leftover Mg2+, and 8 NaOH would need 8 Na+.
x: This counts only the Mg²⁺ in the solid. One Mg²⁺ ion is still dissolved, and it came from the reactants too.
The number of NaOH units equals the number of Na⁺ ions, not the number of Cl⁻ ions. Count the Na⁺ again.
Each Mg(OH)₂ unit contains two OH⁻ ions, and each OH⁻ came from one NaOH.

q: The two boxes show the ions in a sample of HCl(aq) and a sample of Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub>(aq) (water not shown, except water formed by reaction). The samples are mixed and react completely. Which box (I–IV) best represents the mixture after reaction?
h: H⁺ and OH⁻ combine one to one to make H₂O. Find which ion runs out first and what is left over. Spectator ions stay dissolved.
w: The HCl sample has 4 H+ and 4 Cl−; the Ba(OH)2 sample has 3 Ba2+ and 6 OH−. The net reaction is H+ + OH− → H2O, so 4 H+ react with 4 OH− to make 4 H2O, and 2 OH− are left. Ba2+ and Cl− are spectators. Box I shows 3 Ba2+, 4 Cl−, 2 OH− and 4 H2O. Box II shows no reaction, box III leaves H+ instead of OH−, and box IV makes more water than there was H+ to make it.
x: Box II shows the ions just mixed, with no reaction. H⁺ and OH⁻ cannot stay together in large numbers because they combine to form water.
Box III leaves H⁺ over. Compare the 4 H⁺ with the 6 OH⁻ to see which ion is used up first.
Box IV shows 6 water molecules, but only 4 H⁺ ions were present to make water. Hydrogen atoms are not conserved there.

q:
Dichromate ion oxidizes iron(II) ion in acid by the reaction shown. Which statements are true?
I. Fe2+ is the reducing agent.
II. Each chromium atom gains three electrons.
III. H+ is oxidized.
h: Assign oxidation numbers to Cr, Fe and H on both sides. The reducing agent is the species that is oxidized.
w: Fe goes from +2 to +3, so Fe2+ loses electrons, is oxidized, and is the reducing agent: I is true. Cr goes from +6 in Cr2O72− to +3 in Cr3+, a gain of 3 electrons per Cr atom (6 per dichromate ion, matching the 6 Fe2+): II is true. H stays +1 in H+ and in H2O, so III is false. The answer is I and II only.
x: Statement II is true as well. Find the oxidation number of Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻ and compare it with Cr³⁺.
Statement III is false. Hydrogen is +1 in H⁺ and still +1 in H₂O, so it is neither oxidized nor reduced.
Statement III is false. H⁺ supplies hydrogen for the water but its oxidation number does not change.

q: Phosphoric acid, a weak acid, is completely neutralized by sodium hydroxide as shown. What is the net ionic equation?
h: A weak acid is mostly un-ionized in water, so it is written as a molecule. Strong bases and soluble salts are written as ions.
w: NaOH and Na3PO4 are strong electrolytes and split into ions, while H3PO4 is weak and stays as a molecule. Canceling the 3 Na+ spectators gives H3PO4(aq) + 3 OH−(aq) → PO43−(aq) + 3 H2O(l). Writing 3 H+ treats the acid as strong, the single-OH− equation is only the first step of the neutralization, and the Na+ equation describes no reaction at all.
x: This treats phosphoric acid as a strong acid that is fully ionized. A weak acid is written as the intact molecule.
This removes only one H⁺. The equation shows complete neutralization with three NaOH.
Na⁺ and PO₄³⁻ stay dissolved as ions on both sides, so this is not a reaction that takes place.

q: A 0.500 g sample of lawn fertilizer is dissolved in water, and excess BaCl<sub>2</sub>(aq) is added. All of the sulfate precipitates as BaSO<sub>4</sub> by the reaction shown, and the dried solid weighs 0.7015 g. If all of the sulfate came from (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, what is the mass percent of (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> in the fertilizer?
h: Convert the mass of BaSO₄ to moles. One mole of BaSO₄ comes from one mole of (NH₄)₂SO₄.
w: mol BaSO4 = 0.7015 g ÷ 233.39 g mol−1 = 3.006×10−3 mol = mol (NH4)2SO4. Mass = 3.006×10−3 mol × 132.14 g mol−1 = 0.3972 g, and 0.3972 g ÷ 0.500 g × 100% = 79.4%. 57.7% is the percent of sulfate ion alone, 39.7% divides by 1 g instead of the sample mass, and 140.% compares the mass of the precipitate itself with the sample.
x: This is the mass percent of the sulfate ion only. The question asks for the whole ammonium sulfate compound.
Divide by the actual sample mass, 0.500 g, when finding the percent.
A percent over 100 cannot be right. The precipitate is BaSO₄, which must be converted to the mass of ammonium sulfate first.

q: A 25.00 mL sample of an iron(II) solution is titrated with 0.02000 M KMnO<sub>4</sub> in acid by the reaction shown. The purple color first stays after 18.40 mL is added. What is the molarity of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in the sample?
h: Find the moles of MnO₄⁻ used, then use the mole ratio in the balanced equation. Each MnO₄⁻ reacts with more than one Fe²⁺.
w: mol MnO4− = 0.01840 L × 0.02000 M = 3.680×10−4 mol. From the equation, 5 Fe2+ react per MnO4−: 5 × 3.680×10−4 = 1.840×10−3 mol Fe2+. [Fe2+] = 1.840×10−3 mol ÷ 0.02500 L = 0.07360 M. 0.01472 M ignores the 5 : 1 ratio, 0.002944 M divides by 5 instead of multiplying, and 0.1359 M swaps the two volumes.
x: This uses a 1 : 1 ratio. Check the coefficients of Fe²⁺ and MnO₄⁻ in the equation.
This divides by the ratio instead of multiplying. Each MnO₄⁻ consumes several Fe²⁺ ions, so there are more moles of Fe²⁺ than of MnO₄⁻.
The two volumes are swapped. The permanganate volume goes with the permanganate molarity, and the Fe²⁺ moles are divided by the sample volume.

f.text: MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>(aq) + 5 Fe<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + 8 H<sup>+</sup>(aq) → Mn<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + 5 Fe<sup>3+</sup>(aq) + 4 H<sub>2</sub>O(l)

q: 15.0 g of aluminum nitrate, Al(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>, is dissolved in water and diluted to 250.0 mL. What is the concentration of nitrate ion, NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, in the solution?
h: First find the molarity of the salt. Then use the formula: count how many NO₃⁻ ions each formula unit releases.
w: mol Al(NO3)3 = 15.0 g ÷ 213.01 g mol−1 = 0.0704 mol, so the salt is 0.0704 mol ÷ 0.2500 L = 0.282 M. Each formula unit gives 3 NO3−, so [NO3−] = 3 × 0.282 M = 0.845 M. 0.282 M is the salt concentration, 1.13 M counts the Al3+ as well, and 0.0704 is the number of moles, not a concentration.
x: This is the concentration of the salt. Each Al(NO₃)₃ releases more than one nitrate ion.
This counts all four ions from each formula unit. Only the nitrate ions are asked for.
This is the number of moles of salt. Molarity also requires dividing by the volume in liters.

q: A student needs 500.0 mL of 0.150 M HCl and has a stock bottle of 6.00 M HCl. Which procedure is correct?
c: Add 12.5 mL of the stock acid to some water in a 500-mL volumetric flask, then add water to the mark.
Add 12.5 mL of the stock acid to 500.0 mL of water.
Add 75.0 mL of the stock acid to some water in a 500-mL volumetric flask, then add water to the mark.
Add 12.5 mL of water to 487.5 mL of the stock acid.
h: Use M₁V₁ = M₂V₂. The final volume of the solution, not the volume of water added, must be 500.0 mL.
w: V1 = (0.150 M × 500.0 mL) ÷ 6.00 M = 12.5 mL of stock. Diluting it to a final volume of 500.0 mL in a volumetric flask (acid added to water) gives 12.5 mL of stock diluted to the mark. Adding it to 500.0 mL of water makes 512.5 mL, too dilute. 75.0 mL is millimoles of HCl, not a volume of stock, and the last procedure swaps the acid and water.
x: Adding to 500.0 mL of water makes a total volume larger than 500.0 mL, so the solution is a little too dilute.
75.0 is the number of millimoles of HCl needed. It must be divided by the stock molarity to give a volume.
This uses mostly concentrated acid, so the result is far more concentrated than 0.150 M. The stock and water amounts are swapped.

q: Sulfur is recovered from natural gas by the reaction shown. Which statement is correct?
c: H<sub>2</sub>S is the reducing agent and SO<sub>2</sub> is the oxidizing agent.
SO<sub>2</sub> is the reducing agent and H<sub>2</sub>S is the oxidizing agent.
S is the oxidizing agent and H<sub>2</sub>O is the reducing agent.
It is not a redox reaction because sulfur is both a reactant and a product.
h: Find the oxidation number of S in H₂S, in SO₂ and in elemental S. The reducing agent is the reactant that is oxidized.
w: S rises from −2 in H2S to 0 in S, so H2S is oxidized and is the reducing agent. S falls from +4 in SO2 to 0, so SO2 is reduced and is the oxidizing agent: H2S is the reducing agent and SO2 is the oxidizing agent. Agents are always reactants, so products such as S and H2O cannot be the agents. The reaction is redox because oxidation numbers change.
x: The roles are reversed. The oxidation number of S in SO₂ goes down, which means SO₂ gains electrons.
Oxidizing and reducing agents are reactants. S and H₂O are products of the reaction.
Oxidation numbers of sulfur change from −2 and +4 to 0, so electrons are transferred.

q:
Household bleach is made by bubbling chlorine into sodium hydroxide solution, as shown. Which statements are true?
I. Chlorine changes from 0 to −1 in Cl− and from 0 to +1 in ClO−.
II. OH− is the oxidizing agent.
III. Cl2 is both the oxidizing agent and the reducing agent.
h: Assign oxidation numbers to every atom on both sides, including O and H in OH⁻ and H₂O.
w: In Cl2 chlorine is 0; it becomes −1 in Cl− and +1 in ClO− (O is −2): I is true. O stays −2 and H stays +1 in OH−, ClO− and H2O, so OH− is not reduced and is not the oxidizing agent: II is false. Some Cl atoms are reduced and others oxidized, so Cl2 is both agents (a disproportionation): III is true. The answer is I and III only.
x: Statement III is true as well. One Cl atom of each Cl₂ gains an electron and the other loses one.
Statement II is false. Oxygen is −2 and hydrogen is +1 in OH⁻ and in both products, so OH⁻ gains no electrons.
Statement II is false. The oxidizing agent must be reduced, and the atoms in OH⁻ keep their oxidation numbers.

q: The box shows copper atoms from a piece of copper wire in a silver nitrate solution, before any reaction (water not shown). The reaction shown runs until every Ag<sup>+</sup> ion has reacted. What is in the beaker afterward, besides the NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> ions?
c: 3 Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions, 6 Ag atoms and 1 Cu atom
6 Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions, 6 Ag atoms and no Cu atoms
4 Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions, 6 Ag atoms and no Cu atoms
3 Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions, 3 Ag atoms and 1 Cu atom
h: Count the Ag⁺ ions and the Cu atoms. Each Cu atom gives up two electrons, enough to reduce two Ag⁺ ions.
w: The box has 6 Ag+, 6 NO3− and 4 Cu atoms. By the equation, 6 Ag+ need 3 Cu atoms, producing 3 Cu2+ and 6 Ag atoms, and 1 Cu atom is left over: 3 Cu2+, 6 Ag and 1 Cu. Six Cu2+ uses a 1 : 1 ratio, four Cu2+ assumes all the copper reacts, and 3 Ag atoms loses silver.
x: This uses one Cu for every Ag⁺. A Cu atom loses two electrons, and each Ag⁺ gains only one.
Not all of the copper is needed. Six Ag⁺ ions can accept electrons from only some of the Cu atoms.
Silver atoms are conserved. Every Ag⁺ ion that reacts becomes one Ag atom.

q: The box shows the ions in a sample of calcium hydroxide solution (water not shown). How many formula units of sulfuric acid, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, are needed to neutralize this sample completely?
h: Count the OH⁻ ions. Each H₂SO₄ supplies two H⁺ ions, and each H⁺ neutralizes one OH⁻.
w: The box holds 4 Ca2+ and 8 OH−. Neutralization needs 8 H+, and each H2SO4 provides 2, so 4 H2SO4 are needed (Ca(OH)2 + H2SO4 → CaSO4 + 2 H2O). 8 treats the acid as monoprotic, 2 matches H2SO4 to half the Ca2+, and 16 doubles instead of halving.
x: This gives one acid unit per OH⁻. Sulfuric acid is diprotic, so each unit neutralizes two OH⁻ ions.
Each Ca²⁺ comes with two OH⁻. Count the OH⁻ ions, not just the calcium ions.
This multiplies by two instead of dividing. Each H₂SO₄ supplies two H⁺, so fewer acid units are needed than OH⁻ ions.

q: 30.0 mL of 0.200 M FeCl<sub>3</sub> is mixed with 50.0 mL of 0.300 M NaOH, and Fe(OH)<sub>3</sub> (106.87 g mol<sup>−1</sup>) precipitates by the reaction shown. What is the maximum mass of Fe(OH)<sub>3</sub> that can form?
h: Find the moles of Fe³⁺ and of OH⁻. Three OH⁻ are needed for each Fe³⁺, so check which reactant runs out first.
w: mol FeCl3 = 0.0300 L × 0.200 M = 0.00600 mol; mol NaOH = 0.0500 L × 0.300 M = 0.0150 mol. Using all the Fe3+ would need 0.0180 mol OH−, more than is present, so NaOH is limiting. mol Fe(OH)3 = 0.0150 ÷ 3 = 0.00500 mol, and 0.00500 mol × 106.87 g mol−1 = 0.534 g. 0.641 g assumes FeCl3 is limiting, 1.60 g ignores the 3 : 1 ratio, and 0.674 g uses the formula Fe(OH)2.
x: This assumes FeCl₃ runs out first. Check whether there is enough NaOH to react with all of the Fe³⁺.
This uses a 1 : 1 ratio of NaOH to Fe(OH)₃. The equation shows three NaOH per Fe(OH)₃.
This divides the OH⁻ by 2 as if the product were Fe(OH)₂. Iron is +3 here.

q: What volume of water must be ADDED to 40.0 mL of 2.50 M NaOH to make a solution that is 0.800 M? Assume the volumes are additive.
h: Use M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ to find the final volume, then compare it with the starting volume.
w: V2 = (2.50 M × 40.0 mL) ÷ 0.800 M = 125 mL. This is the final volume; the water added is 125 mL − 40.0 mL = 85.0 mL. 125 mL is the final volume, 12.8 mL inverts the ratio of concentrations, and 165 mL adds the starting volume instead of subtracting it.
x: This is the total volume after dilution. The question asks how much water is added to the 40.0 mL already present.
The concentrations are inverted. A more dilute solution needs a larger final volume than the starting 40.0 mL.
The starting 40.0 mL is already part of the final volume, so it should not be added again.

q:
Which of these net ionic equations are balanced for both mass and charge?
I. Zn(s) + Ag+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Ag(s)
II. Cu(s) + 2 Fe3+(aq) → Cu2+(aq) + 2 Fe2+(aq)
III. 2 Al(s) + 6 H+(aq) → 2 Al3+(aq) + 3 H2(g)
h: Count the atoms of each element on both sides, then add up the ionic charges on each side. Both must match.
w: I has matching atoms, but the charge is +1 on the left and +2 on the right, so it is not balanced (it needs 2 Ag+ and 2 Ag). II has a total charge of +6 on each side (2 × 3 = 6; 2 + 2 × 2 = 6) and matching atoms. III has 2 Al and 6 H on each side and a charge of +6 on each side. The answer is II and III only.
x: Statement I fails the charge check. The left side has a charge of +1 and the right side +2.
Statement I is not balanced for charge, even though the atoms match. Electrons lost must equal electrons gained.
Statement II is balanced too. Add the charges: 2 Fe³⁺ gives +6, and Cu²⁺ plus 2 Fe²⁺ gives +6.

q: 0.100 M Pb(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> is added a little at a time to 25.0 mL of a KI solution, and the dried PbI<sub>2</sub> precipitate is weighed after each addition (graph). What was the concentration of KI in the original solution?
h: The graph levels off when all of the I⁻ has precipitated. Read that volume and use the 1 : 2 ratio of Pb²⁺ to I⁻.
w: The mass stops rising at 15.0 mL, so all of the I− is used up there. mol Pb2+ = 0.0150 L × 0.100 M = 1.50×10−3 mol, and 2 I− react per Pb2+, so mol I− = 3.00×10−3 mol. [KI] = 3.00×10−3 mol ÷ 0.0250 L = 0.120 M. 0.0600 M ignores the 1 : 2 ratio, 0.0750 M divides by the combined 40.0 mL, and 0.333 M swaps the two volumes.
x: This uses a 1 : 1 ratio. Each Pb²⁺ removes two I⁻ ions from solution.
The KI concentration refers to the original 25.0 mL sample, not to the combined volume after mixing.
The volumes are swapped. The 15.0 mL goes with the Pb(NO₃)₂ concentration.

q: In the Ostwald process, ammonia is burned over a platinum catalyst as shown. Which element is oxidized, and how does its oxidation number change?
h: Assign oxidation numbers with H = +1 and O = −2 in compounds and 0 in elements. Oxidation is an increase in oxidation number.
w: In NH3, N is −3 (three H at +1); in NO, N is +2 (O at −2). The increase means N is oxidized, from −3 to +2. Oxygen goes from 0 to −2, which is reduction. N cannot be +3 in NH3, and H stays +1 in both NH3 and H2O.
x: Oxygen gains electrons as it goes from 0 to −2, which is reduction, not oxidation.
In NH₃ each H is +1, so N must be negative to make the molecule neutral.
Hydrogen is +1 in NH₃ and still +1 in H₂O, so its oxidation number does not change.

q: Which ions are spectator ions when aqueous barium hydroxide reacts with sulfuric acid as shown?
h: Write the complete ionic equation. Spectators appear unchanged, as dissolved ions, on both sides.
w: Complete ionic: Ba2+ + 2 OH− + 2 H+ + SO42− → BaSO4(s) + 2 H2O(l). Ba2+ and SO42− leave solution as the insoluble solid, and H+ and OH− become water, so no ions are spectators; the net ionic equation is the same as the complete ionic equation.
x: BaSO₄ is insoluble, so Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ leave the solution as a solid. They are not spectators.
H⁺ and OH⁻ combine to form water, so they take part in the reaction.
Ba²⁺ ends up in solid BaSO₄ and OH⁻ ends up in water, so both react.
